senses.definition: (dance) A Brazilian ballroom dance or dance style.
(music) A Brazilian musical genre, to which the aforementioned dance is danced, which has its roots in West Africa via the slave trade.

quotes.text: And when the samba played, the sun would set so high / Ring through my ears and sting my eyes, your Spanish lullaby
quotes.reference: 1986, “La Isla Bonita”, in True Blue, performed by Madonna:

quotes.text: They thought of, I don’t know, monkeys and caipirinhas and samba.”
quotes.reference: 2007 September 20, Eric Wilson, “Blame It on Rio and Gisele”, in The New York Times, archived from the original on 18 Sep 2020:

quotes.text: Slavery was abolished in Brazil in 1888; until then, Bahia had been a major hub of the country’s slave trade. Samba started there for a reason—a fact that Veloso has returned to, obsessively, throughout his career. […] “A samba parade had turned into a brawl,” a reviewer wrote in the Times, adding that the music “suggested a more cool-headed, grown-up epilogue to the shocks of Tropicália.”
quotes.reference: 2022 February 7, Jonathan Blitzer, “How Caetano Veloso Revolutionized Brazil’s Sound and Spirit”, in The New Yorker, →ISSN, archived from the original on 24 Feb 2022:

quotes.text: In front of an audience, he tends to have a freer conversation with himself. The right conditions turn him into an extrovert. He sambas, in the Santo Amaro style.
